title: Engineering Ethics Report: To Ship or Not to Ship
overview: Individual engineering ethics report on the 'To Ship or Not to Ship' scenario. Students analyse Rachel's decision to ship potentially defective servers to a government health department, discuss stakeholder decision-making, argue for and against options using reputable sources and external case studies, and recommend a justified course of action. Report requires abstract, introduction, body, conclusion and consistent referencing; maximum 1,500 words excluding abstract, references and figures/tables.
deliverables: Individual written report on the engineering ethics case 'To Ship or Not to Ship'.
Report containing abstract (~150 words), introduction, body, conclusion, and references.
Discussion addressing: Is this an ethical way to conduct business? How should Rachel determine when to ship a product with known defects and what are the trade-offs? What should Rachel do?
Reference external case studies to support all arguments.
Include a justified recommended course of action.

format.length: Maximum 1,500 words for introduction, body and conclusion combined; abstract around 150 words; references, figures and tables excluded from word count.
format.structure: Abstract (~150 words); introduction; body (may use headings; no restrictions on body organisation); conclusion; references; optional figures and tables.
format.other: Individual written report; consistent established referencing style such as Harvard or IEEE; may refer to relevant course lectures/workshops and Engineers Australia Code of Ethics.

requirements.text: Write an individual report on an engineering ethics case inspired by real-world scenarios faced by engineering professionals, using Topic 2 'To Ship or Not to Ship'.
Identify and discuss ethical issues associated with the scenario.
Explore the ethical dilemmas and consider how stakeholders might make decisions regarding them.
Identify and discuss issues and considerations both for and against decisions, using reputable evidence/sources.
Conclude the report with a justified recommended course of action.

Do not rely only on stating that an action should be taken because a law or regulation requires it; conclusions must be the culmination of thorough research into ethical considerations for all involved stakeholders and holistic discussion of potential consequences.
Address whether this is an ethical way to conduct business.
Address how Rachel should determine when to ship a product with known defects and what trade-offs are involved in decision-making.
Reference external case studies to support all arguments.
Use reputable sources and a consistent established referencing style such as Harvard or IEEE.
May refer to relevant course lectures/workshops; the Engineers Australia Code of Ethics may be worth referencing.
Include an abstract of around 150 words.
Organise the report with an introduction, body and conclusion; headings may be used and there are no restrictions on how the body is organised.
Maximum 1,500 words excluding abstract, references and figures; figures and tables may be used.

Consider the scenario facts: Rachel is a QA engineer responsible for final server testing and part of the team deciding shipment; the company releases a new generation about every six months, limiting QC testing; Rachel will not ship if any possibility of physical harm exists but will ship a higher-likelihood data-loss failure because a competitor would; a government health department contract means failure could cause improper health administration for hospitals/emergency services and catastrophic business consequences; fulfilling it brings significant revenue/growth that can positively affect her employment; large-scale distribution/testing enables safety design improvements for future larger international contracts.
